## How the forecast works {#how}

We forecast all 35 Senate races on 3 November 2026 by combining synthetic voter responses with polling information. We sample 100 personas per state from the 2024 Cooperative Election Study, giving respondents with larger survey weights a greater chance of selection. Each persona receives nine news paragraphs, and four language models answer its voting question three times in their own words. We score these answers using Semantic Similarity Rating (SSR), then average the scores to estimate each state's Republican share of the two-candidate vote.

<!-- DRAFT (Claude): rewrite. -->
Across the polled states, the models' synthetic Republican shares average about 5–9 percentage points above the polling estimates. Our headline method subtracts each model's average synthetic–poll gap before combining its estimate with the state's poll average. We call this bias correction, but the gap is measured against polls, not known election outcomes. Where polls are unavailable, we use the weighted 2024 CES vote share plus the average shift observed in polled states. The noisier of the two estimates gets less weight. This adapts the inverse-variance weighting of Lock and Gelman [@lockgelman2010], but our error estimates are approximate, and polls are not ground truth. We simulate 1,000 outcomes per model, allowing a shared national error to move states together, and give all four models equal weight. Adding the 65 seats not up for election produces a distribution over control of the 100-seat Senate. The [Discussion](#by-method) compares this combined forecast with synthetic-only and no-LLM alternatives.

## Methods {#methods}

The voting responses are synthetic; we did not conduct a new survey. We used Python 3.12 [@python] with pandas [@mckinney2010], NumPy [@harris2020], pyarrow [@arrow], matplotlib [@hunter2007], requests [@requests], lxml [@lxml] and tqdm [@tqdm]. Pilot embeddings used sentence-transformers [@reimers2019]. Tests use pytest [@pytest] and pandera [@bantilan2020], and the website was built with Quarto [@quarto].

### Data {#data}

Our personas come from the 2024 Cooperative Election Study (CES), a survey of 60,000 US adults [@ces2024data; @ces2024guide]. Of these respondents, 38,307 lived in the 35 states holding Senate elections in 2026. Among them, 23,025 had a post-election voter-file weight, and 21,211 were validated as having voted in 2024. We chose the post-election weight because the persona characteristics use both survey waves. A voter-file weight does not by itself show that a respondent voted, so we applied the validated-voter restriction separately.

We obtained candidate lists from Wikipedia on 21 October [@wikipedia2026]. Each race pairs the Republican with the leading Democratic or Independent opponent. Where several names were listed for a side, we selected the candidate appearing most often in polls since 1 August. The opponents in Idaho, Nebraska and South Dakota are Independent. In Montana, Independent Seth Bodnar polls ahead of Democrat Alani Bankhead. The prompts acknowledge additional candidates without naming them individually.

We corrected Montana's candidate pair before the 31 October run. The 27 and 29 October runs paired Republican Kurt Alme with Bankhead rather than Bodnar. Their synthetic estimates and matched polls therefore described a different contest, so those Montana results are not directly comparable with the final run.

Polling data come from PollResults, which compiles Senate polls originally tracked by The New York Times [@pollresults2026]. We use them in the combined forecast and as a benchmark for the synthetic estimates. Polls estimate voter preferences; they are not election results. Their role in setting the weights is described below.

### Personas

Each persona describes a respondent's age, education, race, gender, household income, ideology and party identification. Age is measured in 2024 and grouped as 18–29, 30–44, 45–64 or 65+. Education ranges from less than high school to a postgraduate degree. Race has five categories: White, Black, Hispanic, Asian and Other. Gender distinguishes men, women, non-binary respondents and other responses. Income retains the survey's 16 brackets and its “Prefer not to say” option. Ideology ranges from very liberal to very conservative, while party identification distinguishes strong, weak and leaning partisans from Independents. Uncertain responses are retained as “Not sure.” The models do not see the respondent's reported 2024 presidential vote, which we reserve for descriptive comparisons.

### Weighted sampling

We draw 100 personas in each state, with replacement, giving respondents with larger survey weights a greater chance of selection. Using replacement in every state keeps the procedure consistent, including in Wyoming and Alaska, whose eligible pools contain only 52 and 76 respondents. Across the sample, 904 of the 3,500 personas repeat someone already selected in the same state. About two-thirds of the selections in Alaska and Wyoming are repeats, so 100 personas do not mean 100 distinct people.

Survey weights determine which respondents are drawn; they are not applied again when answers are aggregated. Wang et al. [-@wang2015], by contrast, adjusted an opt-in Xbox sample after collecting responses, using multilevel regression and post-stratification. Our weighted draw reproduces each state's weighted CES composition in expectation, and each selected persona counts equally within its state. Applying the survey weights again would double-weight the sample. The procedure does not account for changes in the electorate between the 2024 presidential election and the 2026 midterms. Equal state sample sizes support separate race forecasts, but pooled demographic comparisons require state-level weighting, as explained in [Crosstabs](#crosstabs).

### News summaries {#news}

We collect news from publisher RSS feeds, with Google News site searches as a fallback. Each collection covers the preceding 48 hours, removes duplicates and keeps up to 60 items per outlet. The ten outlets are The New York Times, The Washington Post, The Wall Street Journal, USA Today, Fox News, New York Post, The Daily Wire, HuffPost, Mother Jones and Vox. We group them as left-leaning outlets, newspapers and right-leaning outlets, following Pew Research Center's audience and political-leaning information [@pew2025sources]. “Newspapers” identifies a source group, not political neutrality.

GPT-4.1 Nano screens titles and feed excerpts for US national significance and relevance to elections, policy, law or the economy. It then writes a short paragraph for each retained item. The instructions exclude sports and unrelated material and require a concrete development. Selected incorrect presidential and vice-presidential titles trigger a rewrite or exclusion. The paragraphs rely on titles and excerpts, not full articles, and the checks do not independently verify their claims.

Each persona receives nine paragraphs, with three drawn at random from each source group. We concatenate the existing paragraphs without another model summary. The same news block is used across models and repeat queries. A fixed random seed reproduces the selection when inputs are unchanged, and retries reuse the dated selections. The tables below describe the retained pool and show one actual persona block, selected for illustration rather than at random.

{{< include data/03-results/comparison/news_summary.md >}}

### Prompts and models

We ask each persona how it would vote in its state's Senate race and randomise the order of the two candidates. Models from four companies allow for systematic differences in their responses [@murray2026]. We record the returned model identifier and query time because a model can change while retaining its advertised name [@bisbee2024].

We use Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-6 Luna, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite through OpenRouter. Each model answers every persona's prompt three times. We score the responses separately and average their scores to reduce variation between individual answers. We request two or three sentences rather than percentages, leave generation temperature at the provider's default, and cap output at 800 tokens. Reasoning is disabled except for Gemini, which requires it and uses minimal effort. Empty, refused and otherwise invalid responses are recorded and excluded from scoring, rather than assigned zero support. Four Claude Haiku calls returned no answer in the 31 October run; calls and answers by model appear in the [cost table](#costs).

### Turning answers into voting probabilities {#scoring}

#### Why free-text answers?

LLM responses can concentrate on a small set of answers, a problem known as mode collapse. Heath and Alexander [-@heath2026] study whether free-text responses scored with Semantic Similarity Rating (SSR) better reproduce distributions in rating tasks. Maier et al. [-@maier2025] introduced SSR for purchase-intent ratings. We use this free-text approach for voting questions, without assuming that it prevents mode collapse.


#### Choosing the embedding model

On 26 October, we compared embedding models on 200 generated answers from Florida personas without news, 50 per voting model. Keyword rules identified 159 answers with a clear candidate choice. MiniLM placed 12 on the opposite side of the two-candidate scale; Gemini Embedding 2 misplaced one. MiniLM's errors involved answers supporting Nixon that also mentioned Moody. Adding both names to each anchor worsened performance, so we retained single-candidate anchors and selected Gemini Embedding 2.

This diagnostic does not validate scoring across all states. Neither setup captured indecision well: answers expressing it received an average weight of 0.14 on the middle category. Leaning and definite statements also often received similar scores. These findings informed the embedder choice while showing the limits of interpreting SSR weights as voting probabilities.


#### Semantic Similarity Rating

Gemini Embedding 2 represents each answer and five candidate-specific statements as numerical vectors. The statements express definite support for the Democratic or Independent candidate, leaning toward that candidate, being undecided or choosing another option, leaning Republican, and definite Republican support. Cosine similarity compares the direction of the answer's vector with each statement's vector, producing five similarity scores per answer.

We rescale those five scores to the range zero to one and apply softmax with a temperature of 0.25. Adding the first two weights gives support for the Democratic or Independent candidate; adding the final two gives Republican support. The middle weight represents other choices, indecision or nonvoting. Answers and statements are embedded in the same way, without separate query and document settings.

These allocations are not calibrated probabilities of an individual's actual vote. Vote choice is not an ordered rating scale, and the middle statement groups behaviours with different meanings. We neither apply a smoothing step nor fit the temperature to voting outcomes, which are not yet observed. This differs from the rating applications in Heath and Alexander [-@heath2026]. Softmax may assign weight to both sides even when an answer clearly names one candidate. That allocation reflects the scoring rule, not greater variation between personas.


### Combining synthetic votes with polls {#combining}

We draw on Lock and Gelman's [-@lockgelman2010] inverse-variance approach to combining forecasts and polls. They estimate predictive uncertainty from past elections. We adapt the weighting idea using approximate error scales for synthetic responses, rather than reproducing their full Bayesian model.

We first average each persona's scores over repeated answers. The state's Republican two-candidate share is the mean Republican score divided by the sum of the mean scores for the two candidates. Resampling personas 1,000 times estimates its bootstrap variability. The outside estimate uses information other than synthetic responses: a state polling average where available, or the weighted 2024 CES vote share plus the average shift in polled states (“2024 plus uniform swing”) otherwise. Polls must name both selected candidates and end within 45 days of the newest poll. We retain one question per poll, prefer likely-voter samples and weight two-candidate shares by sample size.

<!-- DRAFT (Claude): rewrite. -->
The combination has two steps. First, we subtract each model's average synthetic–poll gap across polled states to obtain the corrected share $m^*$. This assumes that polls are correct on average across those states; it does not establish that the original gap was a model error. Second, we combine $m^*$ with the outside estimate $t$: $c=(1-w)m^*+wt$, with outside weight $w=V_m/(V_m+V_t)$. A larger synthetic variance gives the outside estimate more weight. The synthetic variance $V_m$ adds bootstrap variance to a structural variance. We estimate the structural component from the across-state variance of the differences between corrected synthetic shares and polling averages, subtracting the average bootstrap and polling variances. A floor of $0.005^2$ keeps this component positive.

For polls, the error scale adds sampling variance $p(1-p)/n$ to an assumed $0.03^2$ for error beyond sampling [@shirani-mehr2018]. For states without polls, it uses the errors around 2024 plus uniform swing. We draw normal outcomes around the combined share with variance $1/(1/V_m+1/V_t)$, then add a shared national error with standard deviation 0.03. The correction applies each model's average synthetic–poll gap equally to every state. The weights also assume that synthetic and polling errors are independent. These assumptions make the estimates approximate. The [Discussion](#by-method) compares the combined forecast with synthetic-only and no-LLM forecasts, and with a version that retains the gap and counts it as error.

### Sources of uncertainty {#uncertainty}

The simulations account for persona resampling, estimated structural synthetic error after correction, uncertainty in polls or the historical benchmark, and a national error shared across states. Pooling the four models retains their disagreements. However, the average gap, variances and swing are estimated from the same polled states and treated as fixed. We do not separately model regional errors or dependence between synthetic and polling errors. The [sensitivity analysis](#sensitivity) varies the assumed national and polling errors to show their effect on Senate control.

### Tests

Before the full runs, we tested the workflow with five personas per state, free Laguna and Nemotron models, and a local MiniLM embedder. Separate pytest and pandera suites check the simulated data and actual runs. They test individual tables and consistency across the sample, answers, scores and forecasts.

The tests account for expected model–persona combinations and repeats, recorded failures, the returned provider and token usage. Missing or refused answers must remain missing after scoring. Valid scores must lie between zero and one and sum to one. Forecasts must assign valid vote shares and winners, fill all 100 Senate seats and keep the weighted estimate between its two inputs. Another check verifies that the combination uses the saved synthetic estimate and recorded weights.

We checked the tests by introducing missing probabilities, probabilities summing to 1.3, invalid vote-share totals and answers from another provider into a copy of earlier data. Each error was caught. Failed tests stop publication while preserving paid answers. Passing these checks supports consistency of the calculations, not election accuracy.

### Design

We used election coverage from CNN, Politico, NPR, CBC and Reuters as design references [@cnn2024; @politico2024; @npr2024; @cbc2024; @reuters2024]. The website and figures share a colour palette, typography and table style so readers can compare results without relearning the presentation.

### Sensitivity to the assumed errors {#sensitivity}

Our headline forecast assumes a national error with a standard deviation of 3 percentage points and an additional polling error with a standard deviation of 3 percentage points, beyond sampling error. The national component moves states together within each simulation. The polling component affects the uncertainty and weight assigned to polling estimates. These are modelling assumptions, not known error sizes. The table varies both settings to show how much the probability of Republican control depends on them.

## Evaluation {#evaluation}

The forecast cannot be scored against the actual results until after the election on 3 November. Therefore, we compare it with a prediction market that forecasts the same races using a different method.

### Against a prediction market {#markets}

This comparison follows Wang et al. [-@wang2015], who compared their Xbox-based election forecasts with prediction markets before election results were available. We use PredictIt [@predictit2026], which has a market for each of the 35 races and for control of the Senate. It provides another forecast to compare with, rather than ground truth, and combines information through trading [@rothschild2009].

For each news day, we use the daily closing prices returned by PredictIt's API, rather than a live quote. A winning contract pays one dollar, so its price roughly reflects a probability. We normalise the two selected contract prices so that they sum to one: the Republican probability is its closing price divided by the sum of both prices. Third candidates are excluded to match our two-candidate framework. Montana is excluded from the state comparisons on 27 and 29 October because the saved prompts used Bankhead rather than Bodnar (see [Data](#data)); the Senate control comparison retains the full forecast for each day.

{{< include data/03-results/comparison/markets.md >}}

![Our Republican winning probability in each race against PredictIt's, on the latest news day. Points on the dashed line are races where the two agree; points in the shaded corners are races where they favour different sides. Hollow points are races with an independent instead of a Democrat; states that differ by 8 points or more are named.](figures/latest/market_comparison.png){fig-alt="Scatter plot of 35 Senate races, our Republican winning probability against PredictIt's, with a 45-degree line and shaded corners where the two favour different sides."}

## API costs and time {#costs}

Each run uses 3,500 personas. Four models answer for each persona three times, giving 42,000 calls per run. We calculate costs from the recorded token counts using OpenRouter’s list prices as of 25 October. Answer embeddings cost about US$0.50 per run, and news screening costs less than US$0.10. The total estimated cost is about US$9 per run. OpenRouter charged about US$7.20 per run because DeepSeek’s off-peak prices were lower. The total project bill was US$41.38, including the test run and a repeated run. The README lists the charges by day.

{{< include data/03-results/comparison/costs.md >}}

## Discussion {#discussion}

### Comparing synthetic-only, combined and no-LLM forecasts {#by-method}

The table compares four methods using the latest run's saved inputs. Synthetic-only uses the original SSR shares without polling adjustment. The combined forecast, used for the headline, subtracts each model's average gap from polls and combines the corrected shares with state polling averages. Where polls are unavailable, it uses the 2024 CES vote share shifted by the average change in polled states (“2024 plus uniform swing”). The third version combines raw synthetic shares with the outside estimates. Its error scale uses the mean squared synthetic–poll gap instead of the variance of the remaining differences after correction. Both the input shares and weights therefore change. The no-LLM benchmark uses the same polling averages and 2024-plus-swing estimates, excluding synthetic responses. The comparison shows how synthetic responses change the forecast, but cannot establish accuracy before election results are available.

{{< include data/03-results/comparison/methods.md >}}

::: {.chart-note}
The synthetic methods pool four models with equal weight. Seat intervals contain the middle 90% of simulated outcomes.
:::

### Do synthetic voters reproduce partisan voting patterns? {#fidelity}

Argyle et al. [-@argyle2023] define algorithmic fidelity as a model's ability to reproduce patterns of human responses across groups. We compare synthetic Republican support in the 2026 Senate races with the same personas' reported Republican vote in the 2024 presidential election, across demographic and party-identification groups. The prompts did not include that earlier vote. The comparison asks whether the models reproduce earlier partisan patterns, not whether they predict each person's next vote. Because some Senate opponents are Independents, non-Republican support cannot always be labelled Democratic support.

Bisbee et al. [-@bisbee2024] caution that aggregate resemblance can mask overly uniform responses and distorted relationships between characteristics and opinions. The [Crosstabs table](#crosstabs) compares synthetic Republican support with reported 2024 Republican voting across these groups. Party-identification groups help assess whether the models rely too heavily on party, while groups without a clear party preference offer a harder check. Agreement with the 2024 column is not enough: turnout, candidates and preferences can change between elections. We use the tables to describe the synthetic sample, not to validate the forecast.

### Free text and Semantic Similarity Rating {#ssr-discussion}

SSR scores do not always match the strength of support expressed in an answer [@heath2026; @maier2025]. The scoring rule can assign support to both candidates even when a response clearly chooses one. A group can therefore appear less partisan without its personas' answers becoming more diverse. Our limited embedding check also found that undecided answers were not clearly distinguished from candidate support. The forecast depends partly on the reference statements and softmax temperature, as well as on the model answers.

<!-- DRAFT (Claude): rewrite. -->
### The news the personas read

Murray and Alexander [-@murray2026] find that including party identification in a persona can limit the effect of news on its answers. Our [news comparison](#synthetic) shows small changes in the average synthetic share across the recorded runs, with different changes across states. Every prompt includes party identification, which may contribute to this stability. Model answers also vary between runs, so we cannot attribute all changes to news exposure or infer that news has no effect on real voters.

<!-- DRAFT (Claude): rewrite. -->
### Uncertainty and the correlation between states

The [sensitivity table](#sensitivity) shows how error assumptions affect the probability of Senate control. If polls miss support for one party across the country, several closely matched races could change winners together [@gelman2020]. Errors confined to one region may produce patterns that our shared national error does not fully capture. The forecasts change little across the three days, but their wide seat intervals allow many outcomes. Stability alone does not establish accuracy.

<!-- DRAFT (Claude): rewrite. -->
### What agreement with the market tells us

Our forecast and PredictIt agree across many states in the [market comparison](#markets). Much of the high correlation may come from races with a strongly favoured candidate. Disagreements in closely matched races matter more when a few seats could change Senate control. Traders can read the polls used in our combined forecast, so agreement is not an independent check of polling information. Low trading activity and how traders value unlikely outcomes can also affect prices [@rothschild2009; @wang2015]. The comparison provides context; election results are needed to assess accuracy.

### Limitations {#limitations}

We lack results from past elections with which to estimate this synthetic method's typical forecast error. Unlike Lock and Gelman [-@lockgelman2010], we therefore use approximate error estimates rather than historical forecast performance. Polls provide a benchmark, but can miss nonrespondents, misjudge turnout or become outdated as preferences change. Subtracting each model's average synthetic–poll gap can carry a shared polling error into the corrected synthetic estimates. The comparison without bias correction retains the gap and gives synthetic estimates less weight. The [method comparison](#by-method) shows that both the input shares and weighting rules affect the result; neither version is known to be more accurate.

The uncertainty estimates rely on assumptions. As described in [Sources of uncertainty](#uncertainty), estimated error sizes are fixed and not all dependencies are modelled, which may make seat intervals too narrow. The additional polling error has an assumed standard deviation of 3 percentage points, not a value established for these races; the sensitivity table also considers 2 and 4 points. Polls from one aggregator may still share errors [@shirani-mehr2018]. The bootstrap also treats repeated selections of a CES respondent as separate personas. This may understate uncertainty, especially in Alaska and Wyoming, where respondent pools are small.

In the 10 states without usable polls, the outside estimate is the 2024 CES vote share plus uniform swing. A common shift does not account for the appeal of individual Senate candidates. Synthetic estimates may also misrepresent the relationship between demographic characteristics, party identification and candidate choice. In Kentucky, for example, many personas identify as Democrats but describe themselves as conservative. Their synthetic support should not be assumed to measure actual support for the Senate candidates.

The forecast considers only two candidates per race, so the final two-candidate shares do not fully represent other candidates, indecision or nonvoting. In Montana, we compare Republican Kurt Alme with Independent Seth Bodnar and omit Democrat Alani Bankhead. The forecast cannot represent support across all three candidates or how that division affects the winner. Further scoring limitations are discussed under [Free text and Semantic Similarity Rating](#ssr-discussion).

Provider defaults and model updates can change answers even when prompts are saved. News was collected on only three days, limiting what these runs tell us about responses to other events. Future work could vary the amount and mix of news while holding the remaining inputs constant.

Comparable forecasts from more elections would allow us to test the correction and weights. They could also help assess whether error sizes differ by region or race competitiveness, whether models should receive different weights, and whether estimating uncertainty across dates gives more reliable results.

### Conclusion: what the synthetic voters add {#conclusion}

<!-- DRAFT (Claude): rewrite. Numbers from the 31 October run. -->
Synthetic-only strongly favours Republican control, while the combined forecast and no-LLM benchmark favour the Democratic caucus. Synthetic responses change the result relative to the no-LLM benchmark, but receive a small share of the combined weight. The project illustrates how silicon sampling can enter an election forecast; it does not establish an improvement over polling and historical information. Evaluation against election results must use the same vote-share denominator: votes for the two selected candidates, not all candidates. Winner comparisons must also account for omitted candidates who could win or affect the outcome, especially in Montana. Assessing the method more broadly requires more elections and settings.
